Android net Surface × sa_std Gap Census

This page is one volume of the cross-language std census batch (same batch: Rust full std, Go net, Python net, Java net, .NET net, iOS net). Android's “net std” is not isomorphic to desktop platforms: besides the java.net/javax.net.ssl brought by libcore, there is a whole layer of platform connectivity model that does not exist in desktop std (capabilities, metering, multiple networks, system policy). This page counts the two separately: the portable protocol/tool surface is compared against sa_std in four categories, and the platform model is registered separately, not mixed into the gap counts.

Sources and Versions

SideSource
Android public API signature surfaceAOSP platform/prebuilts/sdk, branch android16-release (HEAD 3b7daadc, 2025-04-18), file 36/public/api/android.txt (signature format 2.0) — that is, the exact public API signature inventory of the Android 16 / API level 36 SDK. Newer AOSP's frameworks/base no longer embeds current.txt; the signature surface takes the per-level android.txt in prebuilts/sdk as the authoritative source; the core/java/android/net source of frameworks/base on the same branch (HEAD 99b01a65) serves as supporting evidence.
libcore difference baselineThe public top-level types of the three packages java/net, javax/net, javax/net/ssl in java.base of the desktop OpenJDK source tree (107).
SA-side baselineThe sa_std network surface of sci main 8a943911: 11 .sai contracts with 457 externs in total (net 222, http_client 57, http_server 46, quic 29, ssh 26, tls_client 22, http2 14, ws_client 12, tls_server 11, dtls 11, netx 7), plus 487 fn/macros at the .sa layer (the simplified sa_net_* surface and macro wrappers, noted only, not counted item by item in the comparison).

The NDK/bionic socket layer is POSIX, not Android-specific; it is noted as a boundary and not expanded.

Method and Inventory Scale

Two-side mechanical extraction (scripts and artifacts in tools/android_net_census/, re-runnable): the Android side parses package/class/ctor/method/field declarations from the signature file; the SA side parses @extern declarations from .sai files. The full classification scope totals 323 classes / 1,902 methods / 544 fields (13 packages); the WiFi and Telephony families are registered only (312 classes / 2,069 methods), not classified item by item. The four gap categories use the same methodology as the rest of the batch: directly mappable / needs modeling / model mismatch / existing equivalent.

libcore Differences: Android's java.net vs Desktop OpenJDK

Comparison at top-level class granularity (107 public types on the desktop): Android is missing only two classes, with no Android-only additions —

On desktop, absent on AndroidNature
java.net.UnixDomainSocketAddressAndroid does not expose Unix domain socket addresses through java.net; its equivalent is the platform package's android.net.LocalSocket/LocalSocketAddress (including the abstract namespace, and sa_std's unix surface already covers that shape, including abstract address construction).
java.net.URLPermissionA permission class from the SecurityManager era; Android has no security manager model, so its absence is expected.

Coverage boundary: method-level additions and removals were not compared item by item; for the item-by-item correspondence with desktop java.net, see the Java census page — this page does not double-count.

Platform-Specific Models (a Layer Desktop std Does Not Have)

Network Capability Model

NetworkCapabilities (30 methods, 49 field constants) makes connection “quality” a first-class citizen: capability bits (NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET / VALIDATED / CAPTIVE_PORTAL / NOT_METERED etc., queried via hasCapability), transport types (hasTransport: cellular/WiFi/Ethernet/VPN/Bluetooth), up/down bandwidth estimates, signal strength, subscription ID sets. NetworkRequest.Builder declares requirements with the same capability bits, and the system routes accordingly and reports available/lost/capability changes via ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback callbacks. A desktop std connection lives in a binary “can it connect or not” world; it has no such layer.

Metering and Multi-Network Binding

Metering is a routing input: NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED, ConnectivityManager.getMultipathPreference, getRestrictBackgroundStatus decide background and multipath behavior. Multiple networks are handle-based: a Network object (12 methods) can bindSocket(Socket/DatagramSocket/FileDescriptor) to pin a single socket to a designated network, getAllByName resolves on that network, bindProcessToNetwork / getProcessDefaultNetwork set the process default network; TrafficStats (39 methods) does per-UID traffic attribution and metering. sa_std's connections are a single global stack; this model as a whole belongs to platform services and does not enter the closing shortlist.

Platform-Enforced Policy

Three policies are enforced by the OS and applications can only query or comply: the cleartext policy (android.security.NetworkSecurityPolicy.isCleartextTrafficPermitted() and NetworkSecurityConfig's per-domain configuration decide whether plaintext HTTP is allowed); Private DNS (system-level DoT: LinkProperties.isPrivateDnsActive() / getPrivateDnsServerName() expose the state and server name, the system resolution path carries opportunistic DoT, and DnsResolver queries also go through that path); captive portals and validation (CaptivePortal and the VALIDATED capability bit affect the application-visible “connected” semantics). This is the same kind of platform layer as iOS's NWPath/ATS and can be read in comparison with it.

Coverage Boundaries

  • The member-level inventory is based on the signature file; the first version of the extractor missed declarations whose class headers carry annotations (@Deprecated public class), this has been fixed and re-run (595 → 635 classes / 7,805 members); the rtp/sip packages were exactly this case.
  • libcore differences are at top-level class granularity; method-level additions and removals were not compared item by item.
  • WiFi / Telephony are registered counts only, not classified item by item.
  • android.security is outside the extraction package scope; the existence of the policy section was verified directly from the signature file.
  • Conclusions come only from the actually extracted inventories (tools/android_net_census/out/, checked in with the page); no judgment is made from impressions.
